title: Is sociology losing its place in universities?
text:
I expect to get a lot of grief from some good people about this article (and my post).  The topic is the discipline of Sociology, study of collective human interactions and importantly solutions. Has the discipline become too politicized and activistic to be a scientific discipline in a university? 

The article raises legitimate concerns about ideological conformity within parts of sociology, but it overstates the case by suggesting the discipline has become academically bankrupt. Every field—including economics, psychology, history, and medicine—faces tensions between values and objective inquiry.

Sociology has produced foundational research on social mobility, crime, education, health disparities, family structure, and social networks. Concepts such as social capital, gentrification, and white-collar crime have shaped public policy and influenced multiple disciplines. Much of today's sociology employs sophisticated statistical methods, longitudinal data, and causal inference alongside economics and political science.

Criticism of activist rhetoric within professional organizations is fair, but it should not be confused with the quality of an entire discipline. Enrollment declines reflect shifting student demand for career-focused majors as much as academic shortcomings.

The answer is not to abandon sociology but to reform it: promote ideological diversity, reward methodological rigor, distinguish evidence from advocacy, and encourage open debate. A discipline devoted to understanding society remains too important to be judged solely by its loudest activists.  Many of the critics have their own agenda of course.
